questions.explanation: An absolute phrase has its own subject ('talks' belongs to 'negotiations', not 'they') plus a participle.
options: Negotiations having collapsed, they returned home
Having collapsed the negotiations, they returned home
Collapsed the negotiations, they returned home

questions.explanation: A nominative absolute adds a separate clause-like detail without a conjunction.
The perfect participle shows the searching was completed before the main action.
A present participle at the front expresses a simultaneous or causal circumstance.
questions.q: Choose the correct participial phrase meaning 'because they were exhausted'.

questions.explanation: The absolute phrase gives background with its own subject ('weather permitting').
questions.q: ___ we shall hold the ceremony outdoors.

questions.explanation: A past participle phrase can express a passive reason: 'shocked by the news' = because they were shocked.
The participle clause must attach to the noun it modifies; 'Having finished' attaches to 'she'.
options: Having finished the report, the deadline passed
Having finished the report, she met the deadline
Having finished the report, it was a relief
The report having finished, she met the deadline
questions.q: Choose the sentence WITHOUT a dangling participle.

questions.explanation: 'All things considered' is a fixed absolute phrase meaning 'taking everything into account'.
The perfect passive participle shows the work was finished before the inspection.
A dangling participle attaches to the wrong subject; only one option makes 'the pilot' the one checking.
options: Checking the instruments, the storm worsened
Checking the instruments, it was turbulent
The pilot, checking the instruments, noticed the fault
Checking the instruments, the fault was noticed
questions.q: Which sentence avoids a dangling participle?

questions.explanation: The absolute phrase states a condition with its own subject, more formally than 'if'.
questions.q: ___ we shall meet again next year.

questions.explanation: The participle phrase expresses concession: although granted early release, he reoffended.
Only the absolute construction keeps 'his hands' as the phrase's own subject.
A present participle phrase expresses an accompanying action of the subject.
The passive participle reduces a relative clause: 'the proposals rejected by the board'.
options: the rejected by the board proposals
the proposals rejected by the board
the proposals being rejected by board

questions.explanation: 'There being' forms an absolute phrase with existential 'there'.
The perfect participle clause shows one action completed before the main one.
Only one option has the participle correctly modifying 'the curator'.
options: Hidden for decades, the museum displayed the fresco
Hidden for decades, they displayed the fresco
Hidden for decades, the fresco was finally displayed
The fresco hidden for decades, they displayed it
questions.q: Select the sentence with no dangling participle.

questions.explanation: The absolute phrase with 'with' + noun + participle adds circumstantial detail.
A present participle can replace 'while/when' clauses: 'walking home' = 'while he was walking home'.
